```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
evidence <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "lee_sui_examples.rds",
                                package = "bayesEfron"))
panels <- read.csv(system.file("verification", "panels-convergence.csv",
                               package = "bayesEfron"), check.names = FALSE)
```

In this case study we fit simulated data as we would fit real data, and
then compare the results with the truth. Real data do not allow that
comparison, because the distribution of the true effects is never seen.
Here the true effects of 1,500 sites lie in two separate groups, each
estimate is a true effect plus normal error of a known size, and we give
the model only what an analyst would have: the estimates and their
standard errors. We check whether the fit recovers the two groups, how
well it recovers the individual effects, and what the results depend on.

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

## Two groups of effects and their noisy estimates

The true effects are the 1,500 values of `disjointTheta`, the example
that the deconvolveR package calls Twin Towers [@narasimhan2020]. The
data frame `twin_towers` is one simulated data set from the replication
data of @lee2025, who call such a data set a panel. It is the panel in
which the largest standard error is 9 times the smallest (design
parameters `I = 0.7` and `R = 9`), and the paper uses it in its own
sensitivity analysis of the prior. We use it unchanged. See
`?twin_towers` for the definitions of the design parameters and for the
source.

We call the data `sim` and look at the first rows.

```{r data}
sim <- twin_towers
head(sim)
```

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
low <- sim$theta_true < 0
stopifnot(nrow(sim) == 1500L, sum(low) == 500L,
          max(sim$theta_true[low]) < -0.7, min(sim$theta_true[!low]) > 0.7,
          abs(max(sim$sei) / min(sim$sei) - 9) < 1e-8)
print(range(sim$theta_true[low])); print(range(sim$theta_true[!low]))
```

Each row is a site, and three columns matter here:

- `theta_true` is the true effect. There are `r sum(low)` true effects
  between `r num(min(sim$theta_true[low]), 1)` and
  `r num(max(sim$theta_true[low]), 1)`, and
  `r format(sum(!low), big.mark = ",")` between
  `r num(min(sim$theta_true[!low]), 1)` and
  `r num(max(sim$theta_true[!low]), 1)`. No effect lies between the two
  groups.
- `yi` is the estimate: the true effect plus a normal error with standard
  deviation `sei`.
- `sei` is the standard error. The standard errors run from
  `r num(min(sim$sei), 2)` to `r num(max(sim$sei), 2)` and were assigned
  to the sites at random. For `r num(100 * mean(sim$sei > 1.4), 0)`% of
  the sites the standard error is larger than 1.4, the distance between
  the groups.

Because of this noise the estimates do not show two groups. Their
standard deviation is `r num(sd(sim$yi), 2)`, compared with
`r num(sd(sim$theta_true), 2)` for the true effects. The gap between the
groups is filled in, and the tails reach `r num(min(sim$yi), 1)` and
`r num(max(sim$yi), 1)`. Histograms of the estimates and of the true
effects appear in the plots below.

## A grid from the estimates alone

The model needs a grid of values on which the distribution of effects,
$g$, is defined. In a simulation the range of the true effects is known,
and it is tempting to use it. You could not do that with real data, so we
don't do it here: the call below does not use `theta_true`.

```{r fit-call, eval = FALSE}
fit <- bayes_efron_fit(twin_towers, M = 8, seed = 20250627)
```

We set `M = 8` to get 8 spline functions instead of the default of 6. In
this data set the estimate of $g$ is closer to the true effects with 8,
and the sampler runs more easily. We compare the two settings in the last
section. This is a choice for the example, so don't take it as a
recommendation for large data sets: over 20 data sets of the same design,
the intervals contained somewhat fewer of the true effects with 8
functions than with 6, as we report below.

We ran this fit in advance and stored it in the package as
`twin_towers_fit`, thinned to 1 draw in 15, so the summaries below are
computed from 800 of its 12,000 draws.

```{r stored-fit}
fit <- twin_towers_fit
fit
```

```{r grid-facts, include = FALSE}
grid <- attr(fit$metadata, "grid")
stopifnot(identical(grid$grid_method, "pilot"), grid$pilot$narrowed, grid$M == 8L,
          is.null(fit$metadata$data_list$theta_true),
          grid$support[1] < min(sim$theta_true), grid$support[2] > max(sim$theta_true))
outside <- sum(sim$yi < grid$support[1] | sim$yi > grid$support[2])
print(grid$pilot[c("wide", "share", "seconds")]); print(outside)
```

The `Grid range` line shows how the range of the grid was chosen. In the
output, "rule" means the method chosen with `grid_method`. The default
method, `"pilot"`, works in two steps. It starts from a wide
range, named `"paper_realdata"` in the output: the range of the estimates
widened by half its width on each side, here
`r num(grid$pilot$wide[1], 1)` to `r num(grid$pilot$wide[2], 1)`. That is
far beyond any effect, because the estimates are so much more spread out
than the effects. A short preliminary fit on that range, the pilot fit,
then shows where $g$ lies, and the range is narrowed to that region with
a margin. For these data the result is `r num(grid$support[1], 2)` to
`r num(grid$support[2], 2)`, or `r num(100 * grid$pilot$share, 0)`% of
the wide range. To see the grid we call `plot()` with `type = "grid"`.

```{r grid-plot, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "The eight spline basis functions and the knots of the grid of the fit, over a histogram of the 1,500 estimates, some of which lie outside the grid."}
plot(fit, type = "grid")
```

The upper panel shows the 8 spline functions that are combined to give
the logarithm of $g$. The dashed lines mark the knots and the solid lines
the limits of the grid. The lower panel shows the estimates. All 7
interior knots lie where there are estimates. The `r outside` estimates
outside the grid are not a problem: the grid has to contain the effects,
not the estimates, and an estimate far out in a tail is an effect inside
the grid plus a large error.

## Checking the sampler and the grid

Next we call `diagnose()`, which reports on the sampler and on the grid.

```{r diagnose}
diagnose(fit)
```

```{r diagnose-facts, include = FALSE}
checks <- as.data.frame(diagnose(fit))
ends <- diagnose(fit)$grid$ends
stopifnot(all(checks$status[checks$diagnostic != "grid_ends"] == "ok"),
          checks$status[checks$diagnostic == "grid_ends"] == "note",
          ends$set_by[ends$end == "lower"] == "pilot")
leaning <- ends[which.max(ends$mass), ]
leaning_site <- site_summary(fit, sites = leaning$site)
stopifnot(leaning_site$estimate < grid$support[1])
print(leaning[, c("end", "label", "mass", "set_by")])
print(leaning_site[, c("estimate", "se", "mean")])
```

The sampler passes every check. As `vignette("diagnostics")` explains, a
thinned fit still reports the sampler diagnostics for the whole run, here
12,000 draws.

Among the `Grid` lines there is one thing to look at. Site
`r leaning$label` has `r num(100 * leaning$mass, 1)`% of its posterior
probability in the outer 2% of the grid at the lower end. Its estimate,
`r num(leaning_site$estimate, 1)` with a standard error of
`r num(leaning_site$se, 1)`, lies below that end, and the model cannot
place the effect lower than the grid reaches. `diagnose()` reports this
as a note, because the pilot fit placed that end where the distribution
itself ends. See `vignette("choosing-a-grid")` for what to do about a
note and about a warning.

## The estimated distribution

We plot the estimate of $g$ with `plot_g()`. In a simulation we can pass
the true effects as `truth`, and `normal = TRUE` adds the normal
distribution of a random-effects model fitted to the same estimates.

```{r g-plot, fig.alt = "The estimated density with its band over a histogram of the true effects in two groups, and a dashed normal curve with a single peak near 0.75, at the lower edge of the upper group."}
plot_g(fit, truth = sim$theta_true, normal = TRUE)
```

```{r g-facts, include = FALSE}
g_ci <- confint(fit, type = "g")
rownames(g_ci) <- g_ci$parameter
between <- g_summary(fit, type = "prob", lower = -0.7, upper = 0.7)
# The normal model fitted by REML to the same estimates, as stored with
# the package.
normal_g <- evidence$cases$twin$normal
normal_between <- pnorm(0.7, normal_g$mean, normal_g$sd) -
  pnorm(-0.7, normal_g$mean, normal_g$sd)
stopifnot(g_ci["mean_g", "lower"] < mean(sim$theta_true),
          mean(sim$theta_true) < g_ci["mean_g", "upper"],
          between$mean < 0.1, normal_between > 0.3)
print(between); print(normal_between); print(g_ci[, c("mean", "lower", "upper")])
print(c(mean(sim$theta_true), sd(sim$theta_true)))
```

The gray bars are the true effects, which were not used in the fit. The
solid curve, the posterior mean of the density of $g$, recovers the two
groups: it has a peak over each group and little mass between them. It
does not reproduce their flat tops and sharp edges, because a smooth
curve built from 8 spline functions cannot. The dashed normal curve has a
single peak.

To put numbers on the comparison we use `g_summary()`: first the
probability that $g$ puts between the two groups, then its mean, variance
and standard deviation, which we compare with the mean and standard
deviation of the true effects.

```{r g-numbers}
g_summary(fit, type = "prob", lower = -0.7, upper = 0.7)
g_summary(fit, type = "moments")
c(mean = mean(sim$theta_true), sd = sd(sim$theta_true))
```

The estimate of $g$ puts a probability of `r num(between$mean, 2)` on the
interval from -0.7 to 0.7, which contains no true effect, whereas the
normal distribution puts `r num(normal_between, 2)` on that empty
interval. The mean of $g$ is estimated as
`r num(g_ci["mean_g", "mean"], 2)` (`r num(g_ci["mean_g", "lower"], 2)`
to `r num(g_ci["mean_g", "upper"], 2)`) and its standard deviation as
`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "mean"], 2)` (`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "lower"], 2)` to
`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "upper"], 2)`). The true effects have a mean of
`r num(mean(sim$theta_true), 2)` and a standard deviation of
`r num(sd(sim$theta_true), 2)`.

## Site effects between the two groups

In the plot from `plot_shrinkage()`, each estimate is on the horizontal
axis and its posterior mean on the vertical axis. We
pass `truth` to color the points by their true effects, and
`normal = TRUE` to add a panel for the normal model.

```{r shrinkage, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.8, fig.alt = "Two panels, this fit and a normal model: posterior means against estimates for the 1,500 sites, colored by the true effect."}
plot_shrinkage(fit, normal = TRUE, truth = sim$theta_true)
```

In the left panel the points gather along two levels, because an estimate
is shrunk toward the group that it more probably belongs to. The normal
model in the right panel shrinks every estimate toward a single mean, by
a proportion that depends only on its standard error, and so it places
sites of both groups in the empty middle.

A posterior mean from our fit can fall in that middle too. When a site
has an imprecise estimate between the groups, its posterior distribution
has two modes, and the mean lies between them. We look at two imprecise
sites with `plot_site_posterior()`, and at the most precise site for
contrast.

```{r site-posterior, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Three panels, each with the posterior distribution of a site, the likelihood of its estimate and the estimated distribution of effects. Two imprecise sites have posterior distributions with two modes; the most precise site has a narrow one."}
between_groups <- c(268, 959)
most_precise <- which.min(sim$sei)
plot_site_posterior(fit, sites = c(between_groups, most_precise))
```

```{r site-facts, include = FALSE}
table <- site_summary(fit, sites = c(between_groups, most_precise))
stopifnot(all(table$se[1:2] > 1.9), all(abs(table$mean[1:2]) < 0.5),
          all(table$mode[1:2] < -1), table$se[3] == min(sim$sei),
          all(table$upper[1:2] - table$lower[1:2] > 3.5))
print(table[, c("site", "estimate", "se", "mean", "mode", "lower", "upper")])
print(sim$theta_true[c(between_groups, most_precise)])
```

For sites `r between_groups[1]` and `r between_groups[2]` the likelihood
of the estimate, the dashed curve, is so wide that it covers both groups,
and the posterior distribution retains a part of each. The most precise
site has a narrow likelihood, and its posterior distribution follows it.
The summaries of the three sites come from `site_summary()`.

```{r site-table}
three <- site_summary(fit, sites = c(between_groups, most_precise))
three[, c("site", "estimate", "se", "mean", "mode", "lower", "upper")]
```

The posterior means of the first two sites, `r num(table$mean[1], 2)` and
`r num(table$mean[2], 2)`, are values that the effect is unlikely to
have. Their 90% intervals, more than 3.5 wide, are a better summary, and
the plot is better still. Because of sites like these, `site_summary()`
reports the mode beside the mean.

## Accuracy and coverage

Because the true effects are known, we can check the posterior intervals
against them. We plot the 90% intervals of 150 randomly chosen sites with
their true effects using `plot_recovery()`, which marks the sites with a
true effect outside the interval.

```{r recovery-intervals, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "The 90 percent posterior intervals of 150 sites in the order of their posterior means, with the true effects as crosses and as orange triangles where they lie outside the interval."}
plot_recovery(fit, sim$theta_true, seed = 1)
```

```{r recovery-facts, include = FALSE}
table <- site_summary(fit)
inside <- sim$theta_true >= table$lower & sim$theta_true <= table$upper
rmse <- function(x) sqrt(mean((x - sim$theta_true)^2))
normal <- evidence$cases$twin$normal_metrics
stopifnot(abs(mean(inside) - evidence$cases$twin$compact_metrics$coverage90) < 1e-12,
          abs(rmse(table$mean) - evidence$cases$twin$compact_metrics$rmse) < 1e-10,
          rmse(table$mean) < normal$rmse, normal$rmse < rmse(sim$yi))
defaults <- panels[panels$setting == "defaults", ]
eight <- panels[panels$setting == "M = 8", ]
stopifnot(nrow(defaults) == 1L, nrow(eight) == 1L, defaults$panels == 20,
          abs(defaults$inclusion - 0.9) < 2 * defaults$inclusion_se,
          (0.9 - eight$inclusion) / eight$inclusion_se > 2)
print(c(mean(inside), rmse(table$mean), normal$rmse, normal$coverage90, rmse(sim$yi)))
```

For all 1,500 sites we compute the proportion of true effects inside the
90% intervals, and the root mean squared error (RMSE).

```{r recovery-numbers}
sites <- site_summary(fit)
mean(sim$theta_true >= sites$lower & sim$theta_true <= sites$upper)
rmse <- function(x) sqrt(mean((x - sim$theta_true)^2))
c(posterior_means = rmse(sites$mean), estimates = rmse(sim$yi))
```

The proportion is `r num(100 * mean(inside), 1)`%. The RMSE of the
posterior means is `r num(rmse(table$mean))`, compared with
`r num(rmse(sim$yi))` for the estimates themselves and
`r num(normal$rmse)` for the posterior means of the normal model.

The same function with `type = "calibration"` repeats the first
calculation for intervals of every level from 5% to 95%.

```{r recovery-calibration, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5.4, fig.alt = "The share of the true effects inside the posterior interval against the level of the interval, from 5 to 95 percent, close to the diagonal."}
plot_recovery(fit, sim$theta_true, type = "calibration")
```

The proportions follow the diagonal.

But all of these proportions describe one data set. Coverage is the
mean of such a proportion over repeated data sets, and it takes many data
sets to estimate. Over `r defaults$panels` independent data sets of 1,500
sites from the same design, the mean proportion for the 90% intervals,
which estimates their coverage, is `r num(defaults$inclusion)` (standard
error `r num(defaults$inclusion_se)`) with the default of 6 spline
functions and `r num(eight$inclusion)` (`r num(eight$inclusion_se)`)
with 8. The second value is more than two standard errors below 0.90.
That benchmark is described in `vignette("implementation")`, where the
tables give this mean proportion in a column named `inclusion`. For a
comparison of this fit with empirical Bayes fits of the same data, see
`vignette("empirical-bayes")`.

## Sensitivity to the grid

The stored fit is one of several that we could have made. A table that
comes with the package compares five fits of the same data, each with all
12,000 draws: the call used in this vignette, the defaults, a range
placed around the true effects with 6 and with 8 spline functions, and
the wide range from the estimates alone
(`grid_method = "paper_realdata"`).

```{r ranges}
ranges <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "twin_towers_comparison.rds",
                              package = "bayesEfron"))$table
shown <- data.frame(
  fit = ranges$fit, lower = ranges$lower, upper = ranges$upper,
  tree_depth = ranges$treedepth_share, w1 = ranges$w1, rmse = ranges$rmse,
  inside_90 = ranges$coverage_90
)
shown[-1] <- round(shown[-1], 3)
shown
```

```{r ranges-facts, include = FALSE}
rownames(ranges) <- c("example", "defaults", "truth6", "truth8", "wide")
stopifnot(nrow(ranges) == 5L, all(ranges$max_rhat_parameters < 1.01),
          all(ranges$divergences == 0),
          # With the same number of functions the range around the true
          # effects is the closer one, by less than the step from six
          # functions to eight gains.
          ranges["example", "w1"] > ranges["truth8", "w1"],
          ranges["defaults", "w1"] > ranges["truth6", "w1"],
          ranges["defaults", "w1"] - ranges["example", "w1"] >
            ranges["defaults", "w1"] - ranges["truth6", "w1"],
          ranges$M == c(8, 6, 6, 8, 6),
          ranges["wide", "w1"] == max(ranges$w1),
          ranges["wide", "treedepth_share"] > 0.4,
          diff(range(ranges$rmse)) < 0.01,
          # The table is of the run of 12,000 draws, the stored fit of 800.
          abs(ranges["example", "rmse"] - rmse(table$mean)) < 1e-3)
print(ranges[, c("w1", "treedepth_share", "sampling_seconds", "rmse", "coverage_90")])
```

The table has these columns:

- `lower` and `upper` are the limits of the grid.
- `tree_depth` is the proportion of iterations in which the sampler
  reached its maximum tree depth, a sign that it worked hard for each
  draw.
- `w1` is the Wasserstein distance between the estimate of $g$ and the
  true effects: the area between their two distribution functions, in the
  units of the effects, so smaller is closer.
- `rmse` and `inside_90` are the RMSE of the posterior means and the
  proportion of true effects inside the 90% intervals, as in the previous
  section.

For the estimate of $g$, the number of spline functions matters more than
where the range comes from. With 8 functions, `w1` is
`r num(ranges["example", "w1"])` on the range of this vignette and
`r num(ranges["truth8", "w1"])` on the range around the true effects, and
with 6 functions it is `r num(ranges["defaults", "w1"])` and
`r num(ranges["truth6", "w1"])`. So a range found from the estimates
alone costs some accuracy with either number of functions, but less than
is gained by going from 6 functions to 8.

On the wide range the sampler reaches the maximum tree depth in
`r num(100 * ranges["wide", "treedepth_share"], 0)`% of its iterations,
and the estimate of $g$ is the least accurate of the five. In this data
set, narrowing the range is what makes the default workable.

The posterior means of the sites are almost unaffected by any of this.
Their RMSE differs by less than 0.01 across the five fits. What the grid
changes is the estimate of the distribution and the cost of the fit.
